messages.subject: Re: Blavaan incredible slow...speed-up solutions?
messages.body_plain:
For what it is worth: I too find blavaan extremely slow. A simple model that takes a few minutes in Mplus (with estimator = bayes) takes many hours in blavaan (I gave up once again and forced R to quit).

Sorry for being negative. I've moved back to Mplus, even though I have great respect for free and open-source software. Please note that I use large samples from 1000 to 30,000.

I have also corresponded with Gabe off-list, and we found that some of the default priors on SD parameters were problematic. For example, some of the observed variables ranged from 0-100, so that a gamma(1,.5) on the corresponding residual SD is problematic. Additionally, some priors on regression weights were highly informative, and potentially conflicted with the data.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Maybe it is possible to have blavaan scale all observed variables to have an SD of 1 here, so that the default priors work better. But I worry that it would be problematic for models with certain equality constraints. For example, if you constrain a residual variance to be equal across groups, but then you scale the observed variables, perhaps the constraint leads to a different model than you started with.

messages.body_snippet: For what it is worth: I too find blavaan extremely slow. A simple model that takes a few minutes in Mplus (with estimator = bayes) takes many hours in blavaan (I gave up once again and forced R to qui

messages.subject: Re: Blavaan incredible slow...speed-up solutions?
messages.body_plain:
PS. No problem with lavaan. Fast and good.

For example, some of the observed variables ranged from 0-100, so that a gamma(1,.5) on the corresponding residual SD is problematic. Additionally, some priors on regression weights were highly informative, and potentially conflicted with the data.
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Maybe it is possible to have blavaan scale all observed variables to have an SD of 1 here, so that the default priors work better. I have also corresponded with Gabe off-list, and we found that some of the default priors on SD parameters were problematic. For example, some of the observed variables ranged from 0-100, so that a gamma(1,.5) on the corresponding residual SD is problematic. Additionally, some priors on regression weights were highly informative, and potentially conflicted with the data.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > Maybe it is possible to have blavaan scale all observed variables to have an SD of 1 here, so that the default priors work better. But I worry that it would be problematic for models with certain equality constraints. For example, if you constrain a residual variance to be equal across groups, but then you scale the observed variables, perhaps the constraint leads to a different model than you started with.

messages.subject: Re: Blavaan incredible slow...speed-up solutions?
messages.body_plain:
Can you run this in your set up, and report the system.time() ?
Because I think the porblem is not blavaan, but something on the Stan installation is making the stan models run slow

library(rstan)

scode <- "
parameters {
  real y[2];
}
model {
  y[1] ~ normal(0, 1);
  y[2] ~ double_exponential(0, 2);
}
"

system.time(
  fit2 <- stan(model_code = scode, iter = 10000, verbose = FALSE)
)

messages.subject: Re: Blavaan incredible slow...speed-up solutions?
messages.body_plain:
Mauricio and all,

While the Stan install could definitely be a problem, Christopher's comment about large samples makes me think that blavaan is probably to blame. That reminded me of a sufficient statistic trick that I hadn't gotten around to implementing, so I tried it out yesterday and it really seems to help certain models when there is no missing data. These additions are on github, if you want to try it yourself.

Beyond that, common causes of slowness are prior-data conflict (when priors are informative and conflict with data) and sampling for tens of thousands of iterations (fewer iterations are needed in Stan as compared to Gibbs samplers).

Ed

Ed

thanks

On Friday, April 8, 2022 at 3:32:03 PM UTC+2 Ed Merkle wrote:
> Mauricio and all,
>
> While the Stan install could definitely be a problem, Christopher's comment about large samples makes me think that blavaan is probably to blame. That reminded me of a sufficient statistic trick that I hadn't gotten around to implementing, so I tried it out yesterday and it really seems to help certain models when there is no missing data. These additions are on github, if you want to try it yourself.
>
> Beyond that, common causes of slowness are prior-data conflict (when priors are informative and conflict with data) and sampling for tens of thousands of iterations (fewer iterations are needed in Stan as compared to Gibbs samplers).
>
> Ed

messages.body_plain:
It should work for target="stan", without requiring anything else from you. But right now, it only works for models with continuous variables, complete data, and fixed.x=FALSE. I think you would see the most speedup for large sample sizes (thousands or more).

Ed

messages.subject: prior specification for (i)psi/variance
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have several questions regarding specifying the prior distribution, specifically for (i)psi.

1. This question might be silly but why the default prior for psi is gamma(1,.5)[sd] (or ipsi dgamma(1,.5)[prec])? Or why is it considered as relatively non-informative? Because I thought it's peaked at 0.

2. I'm struggling with the way to specify Cauchy prior/truncated normal prior for (i)psi (in [sd] preferred), either using "jags" or "stanclassic". The point is I want to have a relatively vague prior for variance/psi.
If I understand correctly, the prior distribution can not be changed using "stan". So if I want to use other priors, I should use "jags" or "stanclassic".
For now, I only know something like this would work for truncated normal (many thanks to Ed!): dp=dpriors(ipsi="dnorm(0,1)T(0, )[var]", target = "jags")

2.1. Would it be possible to specify it on [sd] instead of [var]? I tried but I got error like this:
[1] "Error in ivs[ivs <= 0] <- -ivs[ivs <= 0] : \n  NAs are not allowed in subscripted assignments\n"
attr(,"class")
[1] "try-error"
attr(,"condition")

2.2.  And I checked in this group using Cauchy prior like this: dt(0,1/2.5,1)T(0,)[sd], but again it didn't work and got error like this:
[1] "Error in ivs[ivs <= 0] <- -ivs[ivs <= 0] : \n  NAs are not allowed in subscripted assignments\n"
attr(,"class")

In addition: Warning messages:

  NAs introduced by coercion
2: In rnorm(n, ncp) : NAs produced

Many thanks in advance!
Best,
Hongwei

messages.subject: Re: prior specification for (i)psi/variance
messages.body_plain:
Hongwei,

The default psi prior is set to gamma because it often works well, but you are right that it will not always work. I am considering changing the default to something that involves the data. For example, you look at the total variance of each variable, then set a distribution that places most density between 0 and the value of the total variance. That seems like a decent default.

About the [sd] thing: it should be possible and looks like a bug. I will explore it some more.

Ed

messages.subject: blavaan and MplusAutomation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

We are running a Bayesian Path Analysis with a binary outcome for a dataset
with more than 1 million rows. We were not able to fit our model using blavaan
package, but we were able to do it using Mplus. However, we would like to use
blavPredict() function.

Do you know whether it is possible to use the results from models fitted
in MPlus and read them as objects in blavaan package after having used the
MplusAutomation package that allows us to read, run and extract model summaries
from analyses performed using Mplus?

When trying to make use of the blavPredict(), we got the following error
message:

> ypred <- blavPredict(test, type = "ypred")

Error in blavPredict(test, type = "ypred") :

  inherits(object, "blavaan") is not TRUE

Best regards,

             Leila

messages.body_plain:
> right now, it only works for models with continuous variables, complete data, and fixed.x=FALSE.

Would the same trick work if implemented per missing-data pattern?  Perhaps problematic for unplanned missingness incomplete, but from planned-missing designs, it can be possible to compute the summary stats for the subset of variables relevant per missing pattern.  Vika and Ke-Hai capitalized on that for one of their proposed model-based transformation methods (extending Bollen-Stine for incomplete data).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Blavaan incredible slow...speed-up solutions?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, it should work for missing data but I think will require a custom lpdf in Stan. The problem is that you get to a missing data pattern with 1 observation, and the sample covariance matrix for that pattern is not positive definite, and then Stan throws an error when you try to model it. I think you can get around it by avoiding the constant terms in the density function.

Ed

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ed,

I'm seeking some clarification on what this function you provided above does in comparison with blavPredict(data, type = "ypred").  blavPredict "ypred" is conditioning on the sampled latent variables, and the blavaan documentation says to use postdata() if one is interested in posterior predictives that do not condition on the latent variables (I can't find postdata(), though, so I'm also wondering if that's available yet). The code above is "including" latent variables in the posterior distributions it creates, so I'm just wondering whether the code above is more like postdata() or blavPredict("ypred")?

I used the code you provided above to plot posterior distributions from the cfa above (for variable "x1"), and I did the same thing with blavPredict("yred"), and the distributions of the posteriors look slightly different (image attached; R code below). The means of each distribution are nearly identical, but blavPredict has a larger SD for each distribution, so I am assuming these two methods of getting posteriors are doing different things, I'm just not clear on what differs between the methods.

Thank you for your input!
Garret

library(blavaan)
library(tidyverse)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- bcfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, burnin=100, sample=100, save.lvs=TRUE)

# recommendation from Ed Merkle to get posterior distribution

psamps <- do.call("rbind", blavInspect(fit, 'mcmc'))

lvsamps <- do.call("rbind", blavInspect(fit, 'lvs'))

cmns <- lapply(seq(nrow(psamps)), function(i){
  lavmodel <- blavaan:::fill_params(psamps[i,], fit@Model, fit@ParTable)
  eta <- blavaan:::fill_eta(lvsamps[i,], fit@Model, fit@ParTable,
                            fit@SampleStats, fit@Data)
  lavaan:::computeYHAT(lavmodel, lavmodel@GLIST, fit@SampleStats, ETA = eta)
})

#blavPredict
pred <- blavPredict(fit, type = "ypred")

#plot the data
pred2 <- bind_rows(lapply(pred, as.data.frame), .id = "df")
cmns2 <- bind_rows(lapply(cmns, as.data.frame), .id = "df")
cmns2$type <- "Ed's code"
pred2$type <- "blavPredict 'ypred'"
cmns2 <- cmns2 %>% rename(x1 = X1,
                          x2 = X2,
                          x3 = X3,
                          x4 = X4,
                          x5 = X5,
                          x6 = X6,
                          x7 = X7,
                          x8 = X8,
                          x9 = X9)
allpred <- rbind(cmns2, pred2)

allpred %>% ggplot(aes(x = x1, group = df)) + geom_density() + facet_wrap(~type)

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the report, and I just pushed a fix to github that should allow for these truncated priors in target="jags". The problem involved starting values, so if you have a similar problem in the future, try adding

inits = "simple"

when you run the model.

Ed
